deep.reconstruction:
This page is not a Riemann manuscript and contains no derivations. It is the first page of a letter in German, dated 'Dresden, d. 12. Aug. 1891', 25 years after Riemann's death. It is filed in the Riemann Nachlass bundle on P-functions. The writer is a Dresden mathematician who has written a 'historischer Aufsatz' (historical essay) on the subject. The plausible candidate is Erwin Papperitz, at the Dresden Polytechnikum from 1885, who worked on Riemann P-functions; this is an inference, since the signature is not on this page. The recipient, addressed as 'Hochverehrter Herr Professor', is likely the editor of Riemann's works, which suggests Heinrich Weber (2nd edition of the Werke, 1892). The recipient is not named.

Content of the page:
(1) Besides Thomae, Pochhammer had earlier treated the representation of hypergeometric functions by integrals along complex paths. The writer believes Pochhammer published an article about 8 years earlier in the Zeitschrift für Mathematik und Physik, but cannot check because the library is closed for revision.
(2) More important, the question has been brought to a fully satisfactory conclusion by two papers:
- Pochhammer, 'Ueber ein Integral mit doppeltem Umlauf', Math. Ann. 35.
- F. Klein, 'Ueber Normirung der linearen Differentialgleichungen zweiter Ordnung', Math. Ann. 38, which partly builds on Pochhammer's.
(3) On Thomae's work, which the recipient says is open to certain objections: the writer has not tried to apply Thomae's method. The writer's view is that Thomae's normalization of the integrals is not what Riemann had in mind. The sentence continues on the next page: Thomae only makes the first coefficient of each branch expansion equal to 1.

Mathematical context, mine and not on this page: the Pochhammer double-loop contour P(a,b) makes the Euler-type integral of t^(α-1)(1-t)^(β-1) valid for all exponents. Its value is (1-e^{2πiα})(1-e^{2πiβ}) B(α,β). Klein used such integrals in homogeneous variables to fix a canonical normalization of the branches of the P-function. Riemann's own 1857 P-function paper leaves the constant factors of the branches unnormalized.
errors: No mathematical steps on this page, so none can be in error.
Archival point: this is an 1891 letter by a third party, not a Riemann autograph, despite being foliated in the Riemann P-Functionen bundle.

The writer's recollection of a Pochhammer article in the Zeitschrift für Mathematik und Physik 'about 8 years ago' is hedged by the writer himself. I am unsure of the exact reference. The other two citations (Pochhammer, Math. Ann. 35; Klein, Math. Ann. 38) match the known papers.
